bib.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 13 of 13 pages, 43,962 of 43,962 chars, main text, appendices A-C and references. No extraction faults. Figures 1-6 are graphics, so their plotted values were not read.

AUTHORS: Zhihao Zhan*, Ting Song*, Li Dong†, Shaohan Huang, Jianxun Lian, Yan Xia†, Furu Wei† (* equal contribution, † corresponding). Microsoft Research.
VENUE: arXiv preprint, "Technical report", arXiv:2609.26781v1 [cs.CL], 22 Sep 2026. The repo is github.com/microsoft/Agensh.

CORE CLAIM: A harness with no central orchestrator can scale to many agents. Workers run a five-step loop: gather context, claim a sub-task, act, verify, merge. They coordinate through three shared pieces: a Git workspace (Gitea), a chat interface (Mattermost) and an append-only "shared context" board (idea taken from DeLM). The authors argue agent count is a new scaling dimension for multi-agent organizations.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- Setup for all of them:
  - Model and harness: GPT-5.6-sol (high reasoning), Copilot as the single-agent harness, 272k input and 128k output token limits.
  - Task: the 5 hardest of ProgramBench's 200 tasks (FFmpeg, gromacs, pandoc, PHP-src, ctags), each rebuilt from scratch with no internet.
  - Budget: 6h per run, scored as canonical-kept pass rate.
- Mean pass rate across the 5 tasks, by agent count:
  - 1 agent: 19.31%
  - 8 agents: 20.68%
  - 32 agents: 26.52%
  - 128 agents: 28.78%
  - That is +9.47 points, about a 49% relative gain.
- Latency: on pandoc, 128 agents pass 30% at the 30-minute checkpoint. 32 agents get there at 60 minutes and 8 agents at 90 minutes. A single agent stays below 30% for the first 2h.
- Pandoc alone, by agent count: 1 agent 33.89%, 128 agents 50.94%, 1,024 agents 55.06%. Going from 128 to 1,024 adds 4.12 points. 1,024 agents ran across 16 nodes, 64 per node.
- Emergent behaviour from trajectory reading, anecdotal and not counted:
  - 8 agents agree on interfaces and resolve overlapping claims.
  - 32 agents review and approve each other's work and withdraw approvals.
  - 128 agents choose reviewers by experience and settle on a reusable integration protocol.
  - 1,024 agents have several workers acting as integrators.

ABLATION: None. The only comparison is agent count. Nothing isolates the shared context, the messaging or the Git workspace. There is no comparison against an orchestrator-worker harness.

QUOTES
- p.6: "Scaling from 1 to 128 agents yields a gain of 9.47 percentage points, or an approximately 49% relative improvement in the average score."
- p.2: "the scalability of the overall system remains fundamentally limited by the orchestrator's capacity to manage and coordinate its workers and integrate their contributions"
- p.7: "Surprisingly, these forms of cooperation are entirely self-organized: workers themselves choose collaborators, divide responsibilities, and establish and revise their workflows through peer interactions." (The page 7 text is the cooperation-emergence passage that ends on p.8. Check the page before citing.)
- p.12 (App. A prompt): "FAIL for a hypothesis you falsified (the highest-value entry: it stops peers spending budget on it)"

LIMITS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW
- The report gives no cost or token spend, no number of runs and no variance. The figures appear to be single runs per cell.
- It does not show that the orchestrator is the bottleneck. The claim is asserted and cited to [10-12], and there is no orchestrator baseline.
- Only one benchmark family (ProgramBench, software reproduction), one model and one harness. The 1,024-agent run is on one task (pandoc).
- Gains flatten: 8 agents add only about 1.4 points, and 128 to 1,024 adds 4.12 points for 8x the agents.
- Efficiency per agent is not measured. Duplicated work and failure modes such as conflicts, wasted claims and stalled agents are not quantified.
- The 1-agent baseline needed a stop hook so it would run the full 6h. Scaled runs used staggered starts (one agent every 30s for the first hour, then every 3s) and reminders at T-45 min and T-5 min. The authors disclose all of this.
- The paper makes no claim about subagents as context firewalls, role separation, or when not to go multi-agent.

BUILDS ON
- ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023) for the single-agent loop.
- DeLM, "Decentralized multi-agent systems with shared context" (Mao and Mirhoseini, arXiv 2606.10662, 2026) for the shared context.
- Carlini's C compiler built by 16 parallel Claudes, using Git and task-lock files (Anthropic Engineering Blog, Feb 2026).
- Kim et al., "Towards a science of scaling agent systems" (arXiv 2512.08296, 2025).
- Anthropic's multi-agent research system (Jun 2025) and "Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems" (Aug 2026).
- AgentNet (NeurIPS 2025), STORM (arXiv 2605.20563), ProgramBench (arXiv 2605.03546, 2026), ChatCollab and SlackAgents.

PLACEMENT: 07-orchestration fits, and it fits best as a contrast case: no orchestrator, and peer topology at scale. The topologies, asynchronous agents and handoffs sections are the closest match. A secondary fit is 02 anatomy, for the shared-state parts (append-only board with typed entries, Git workspace, event-driven runtime, idle detector). Nothing in it fits 03, 04 or 08. Treat it as a vendor-style preprint with a single-benchmark scaling curve. It is weak evidence for general claims and should be cited cautiously (sharpens or contrasts, not as a rule).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 3 (p.3), the cooperation loop with workers on top and the shared workspace, message interface and shared context below. It explains the design faster than prose. Figure 2 is the alternative, orchestrator versus self-organized.
